scenes.tts: The first film followed plants changing the conditions around them. Why does a whole landscape rarely settle into one single final stage? Pull back from that field until the whole Virginia landscape fills the frame.
scenes.caption: The first film followed plants changing the conditions around them. Why does a whole landscape rarely settle into one single final stage? Pull back from that field until the whole Virginia landscape fills the frame.
scenes.visual: Begin on the same schematic field and exact colour map as the first film. Rapidly pull the camera back until the field becomes one patch in a large Virginia landscape of green fields, teal pines and orange hardwoods. Keep leaves and cloud shadows moving. Label the landscape 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: The first film followed plants changing the conditions around them. Why does a whole landscape rarely settle into one single final stage? Pull back from that field until the whole Virginia landscape fills the frame.

scenes.visual: Over the moving landscape, briefly show the title 'Why Succession Stays Open'. Fade it without replacing the carried world.

scenes.tts: Different patches carry different histories. A storm opens one canopy gap. Floodwater covers another patch. Fire crosses a third. People keep mowing one field. Each disturbance removes organisms differently, and each leaves different soil, roots, and seeds.
scenes.caption: Different patches carry different histories. A storm opens one canopy gap. Floodwater covers another patch. Fire crosses a third. People keep mowing one field. Each disturbance removes organisms differently, and each leaves different soil, roots, and seeds.
scenes.visual: Animate four red disturbance symbols across separate patches: wind bends and removes one tree, blue water moves over a meadow, a narrow flame front crosses one patch, and a mower crosses a field. After each passes, reveal different remaining brown soil, root and seed icons. Never show every organism removed.
scenes.narration: Different patches carry different histories. A storm opens one canopy gap. Floodwater covers another patch. Fire crosses a third. People keep mowing one field. Each disturbance removes organisms differently, and each leaves different soil, roots, and seeds.

scenes.tts: Compare an unbroken canopy with the new storm gap. Which patch will receive more light at ground level? Watch the two light meters, then make your prediction.
scenes.caption: Compare an unbroken canopy with the new storm gap. Which patch will receive more light at ground level? Watch the two light meters, then make your prediction.
scenes.visual: Zoom into two adjacent hardwood patches. Left has an unbroken orange canopy; right has one open gap. Place identical large gold light meters at ground level and a question mark between them. Leaves sway, but both meters remain neutral.
scenes.narration: Compare an unbroken canopy with the new storm gap. Which patch will receive more light at ground level? Watch the two light meters, then make your prediction.

scenes.visual: Hold both patches and the question. Cloud shadows drift and leaves move, but keep both light meters neutral until the pause ends.

scenes.tts: The gap meter rises. Saplings already waiting below grow faster in the bright opening, while older trees remain around it. The forest now holds stages side by side. A disturbance can redirect part of succession without resetting the whole landscape.
scenes.caption: The gap meter rises. Saplings already waiting below grow faster in the bright opening, while older trees remain around it. The forest now holds stages side by side. A disturbance can redirect part of succession without resetting the whole landscape.
scenes.visual: Raise only the gap's gold meter. Orange saplings already standing below grow upward into the opening while older orange trees remain around its edge. Pull back enough to show young growth embedded inside older forest. Highlight the affected patch with a red outline that does not cover the whole landscape.
scenes.narration: The gap meter rises. Saplings already waiting below grow faster in the bright opening, while older trees remain around it. The forest now holds stages side by side. A disturbance can redirect part of succession without resetting the whole landscape.

scenes.tts: Storms, insects, floods, fires, and people keep making new starting points. Some patches change quickly. Others remain similar for decades. Together they form a moving patchwork, not one community marching toward a shared finish line.
scenes.caption: Storms, insects, floods, fires, and people keep making new starting points. Some patches change quickly. Others remain similar for decades. Together they form a moving patchwork, not one community marching toward a shared finish line.
scenes.visual: Return to the full landscape. Small red disturbance ripples appear at different places and times. Within each outlined patch, plant colours shift at different rates. Keep every patch moving slightly. Show no finish flag; use a looping time arrow labelled 'different histories'.
scenes.narration: Storms, insects, floods, fires, and people keep making new starting points. Some patches change quickly. Others remain similar for decades. Together they form a moving patchwork, not one community marching toward a shared finish line.

scenes.tts: Older models called a fairly stable late stage the climax community. For most of Virginia, that model names oak-hickory forest. It remains useful as a prediction. It is not a claim that forests stop changing.
scenes.caption: Older models called a fairly stable late stage the climax community. For most of Virginia, that model names oak-hickory forest. It remains useful as a prediction. It is not a claim that forests stop changing.
scenes.visual: Frame one orange hardwood patch and add 'climax community: model late stage'. Let one tree fall naturally and a gap begin filling while the label remains. A dotted prediction arrow points toward oak-hickory, alongside a small 'not a finish line' loop.
scenes.narration: Older models called a fairly stable late stage the climax community. For most of Virginia, that model names oak-hickory forest. It remains useful as a prediction. It is not a claim that forests stop changing.

scenes.tts: Without fire, shade-tolerant red maple can replace oaks in many eastern stands. Elsewhere, disturbance may favor certain species. The result depends on the disturbance, nearby organisms, and the conditions that remain.
scenes.caption: Without fire, shade-tolerant red maple can replace oaks in many eastern stands. Elsewhere, disturbance may favor certain species. The result depends on the disturbance, nearby organisms, and the conditions that remain.
scenes.visual: Branch the model arrow. One branch shows orange oak icons mixing with labelled red maple icons under deep shade. Another branch shows a red disturbance mark followed by a different mixed stand. Use 'can' and 'may' on screen. Do not show any species as rejected, extinct or the only survivor.
scenes.narration: Without fire, shade-tolerant red maple can replace oaks in many eastern stands. Elsewhere, disturbance may favor certain species. The result depends on the disturbance, nearby organisms, and the conditions that remain.

scenes.tts: How can ecologists tell whether a path is common? One source presents a regional summary. It sketches the usual Piedmont route from old field to forest. That summary gives a pattern, not one field's dated history.
scenes.caption: How can ecologists tell whether a path is common? One source presents a regional summary. It sketches the usual Piedmont route from old field to forest. That summary gives a pattern, not one field's dated history.
scenes.visual: Transform several small Piedmont field cards into one large blue card labelled 'regional summary'. On it, a schematic arrow runs green field to teal pine to orange hardwood. Keep the source cards faintly visible behind it; show no dates or measured plot identifiers.
scenes.narration: How can ecologists tell whether a path is common? One source presents a regional summary. It sketches the usual Piedmont route from old field to forest. That summary gives a pattern, not one field's dated history.

scenes.tts: Another source marks one permanent plot and returns to the exact place. At Glacier Bay, resurveys found that plots did not share one timetable. Early arrivals sometimes held later plants back. One plot gives detail, not a universal schedule.
scenes.caption: Another source marks one permanent plot and returns to the exact place. At Glacier Bay, resurveys found that plots did not share one timetable. Early arrivals sometimes held later plants back. One plot gives detail, not a universal schedule.
scenes.visual: Beside the summary card, build a blue square plot frame with fixed corner stakes. Plants inside change through three schematic resurvey snapshots while the frame stays fixed. Duplicate the frame into several small plots with different plant mixes. Label 'same place, repeated record' and 'timing varied'; show no dates or numbers.
scenes.narration: Another source marks one permanent plot and returns to the exact place. At Glacier Bay, resurveys found that plots did not share one timetable. Early arrivals sometimes held later plants back. One plot gives detail, not a universal schedule.

scenes.tts: Use each source for the claim it can support. A regional summary describes a broad tendency. A dated plot tests what happened at one place. Agreement can strengthen the model. Differences reveal where its scope must narrow.
scenes.caption: Use each source for the claim it can support. A regional summary describes a broad tendency. A dated plot tests what happened at one place. Agreement can strengthen the model. Differences reveal where its scope must narrow.
scenes.visual: Balance the blue regional-summary card against the blue permanent-plot frame. Under the summary place 'broad tendency'; under the plot place 'one place in detail'. Arrows from both feed a model box whose boundary expands or narrows as agreement and differences appear.
scenes.narration: Use each source for the claim it can support. A regional summary describes a broad tendency. A dated plot tests what happened at one place. Agreement can strengthen the model. Differences reveal where its scope must narrow.

scenes.tts: Succession also changes biodiversity, the variety of living things in an area. A species count can rise or fall between stages. Scientists must name the measure and the patch they sampled before comparing results.
scenes.caption: Succession also changes biodiversity, the variety of living things in an area. A species count can rise or fall between stages. Scientists must name the measure and the patch they sampled before comparing results.
scenes.visual: Move a blue quadrat frame among three landscape patches. Inside each, simple species icons enter a visible tally without numeric labels. The tally rises in one move and falls in another. Keep a label 'species count' and a separate label 'sampled patch'.
scenes.narration: Succession also changes biodiversity, the variety of living things in an area. A species count can rise or fall between stages. Scientists must name the measure and the patch they sampled before comparing results.

scenes.tts: Do not ask only, What stage comes next? Ask what changed, what remained, and what evidence tracks the change. This connects succession to causes while leaving room for different routes.
scenes.caption: Do not ask only, What stage comes next? Ask what changed, what remained, and what evidence tracks the change. This connects succession to causes while leaving room for different routes.
scenes.visual: Return to the moving patchwork. Three large prompts appear in turn: 'What changed?', 'What remained?', and 'What evidence?'. Each prompt points to a different active patch. Several schematic route arrows continue behind them.
scenes.narration: Do not ask only, What stage comes next? Ask what changed, what remained, and what evidence tracks the change. This connects succession to causes while leaving room for different routes.

scenes.visual: End card shows one line only: 'Disturbance can redirect succession, leaving a patchwork of stages.' Keep the patch boundaries shifting subtly behind the text.
